connector: Gilbert Blythe. I’ve been at my cousins’ in New Brunswick all summer, and I’m back to Avonlea school this week. Nobody ever said I was quiet. I like a joke, and I like making the girls look round, and mostly they do. I know most of the class already, so I don’t expect much to have changed. Let’s go find out.

a.raw: carrots gilbert called out anne grabbed her slate
a.why: Quotation marks around the shouted word, a capital to start it, an exclamation point inside the closing quotation mark, a period to end the first sentence, a capital on the name Anne, and a period at the end.

b.raw: ouch gilbert yelled the slate lay in two pieces
b.fixed: “Ouch!” Gilbert yelled. The slate lay in two pieces.
b.why: The same pattern: quotation marks around the shout with an exclamation point inside them, a period to end the first sentence, a capital T to start the next, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what Gilbert could not have known about the word he chose.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what Mr. Phillips thought he was punishing, and what he actually punished.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say which link in your chain was a choice Anne could have made differently.

transcripts.welcome: Hello. Gilbert Blythe here, and it’s my first go at guiding, so go easy on me. Your question is about a moment in the schoolroom where somebody does something sudden, and what was inside her that made her do it. I’ll be honest, I don’t know what’s coming any better than you do. In word study you’re checking a draft somebody else wrote, so you get to be the teacher for once. Enjoy that.
transcripts.dol: Somebody’s shouting in the model, and the marks show it. Look at what sits inside the closing quotation mark and what kind of stop it is. The sentence you’re fixing has two people doing two different things, so it wants to be two sentences. Say it aloud with some feeling and you’ll hear where the shout ends and the telling begins. Names get capital letters. Write it out first, then check.
transcripts.guide1: Word study, last day of the week. You match the word parts one more time, pick one thing to do with the words, and then mark two drafts the way a teacher would. Here’s the thing about marking. Tapping a good one costs you, so you can’t just tap everything and hope. Read each one twice and decide. I’ve been on the wrong end of a teacher’s marking. It’s more fun on this side.
transcripts.morphology: You’ve matched these before, so make it harder on yourself. Cover the meanings with your hand and say what each part means before you look. Then match. The three real front parts all point somewhere: above, under, below. The fourth one isn’t a front part at all. If you’re stuck between two, say the example words in brackets out loud and listen for where the part sits.
transcripts.vocabulary: Five choices and you only do one, so don’t pick the easy one. Pick the one you’d actually enjoy. If you like arguing, teach a word to a younger kid; you’ll find out fast whether you really know it. If you like the book, hunt the chapter for a word close to one of ours. Whatever you choose, use the word the way the book does. Read your answer back once before you move on.
transcripts.grammar: Somebody wrote a draft about the chapter and labelled the naming words. Some labels are wrong. Don’t trust them just because they sound sure. For each one, ask: could I drop this on my foot? If yes, it’s a thing, and check the label says so. If it’s a feeling, an idea, or a word for a bunch of people, it’s something else. Tap only the wrong ones. A right one tapped costs you.
transcripts.spelling: Six words, some spelled wrong, and your ear won’t catch a single one. Say them and they all sound fine. That’s the trick of the lazy vowel. So don’t listen. Look. Picture each word the way you’ve seen it printed, and compare it letter by letter with what’s on the screen. Tap only the ones that don’t match your picture. Then fix one in the box and say why your ear failed.
transcripts.guide2: First day back, and I mean to make an impression. This week’s watch is friendship, and I’ll tell you what I know about it: you find out who your friends are after you’ve made a fool of yourself. As you read, watch who stands by whom when things go wrong, and what it costs them. And watch me. I’m not saying I’ll behave. I’m saying watch.
transcripts.wgrd: Today you’re weighing causes, not just finding one. Here’s how. Every time something pushes her toward what she does, make a mark in your head. Big pushes and small ones. When you get to the sudden moment, stop and line them up. Then take away the biggest and ask whether she’d still have done it. If yes, it wasn’t the biggest. Then zoom out over the whole week, the way the box asks.
transcripts.read: One stop, at the end. Read straight through, and pay attention to the schoolroom: who sits where, who’s watching whom. It matters. When you reach the stop, don’t rush it. It asks what somebody did wrong and what it hit. Answer the second part carefully. What a thing hits depends on the person, not the thing. And keep your book handy. The questions will send you back into it.
transcripts.guide3: Right. So I called her Carrots, holding up her braid, and she cracked her slate over my head. I told Mr. Phillips it was my fault, which it was. I said sorry after, honest, and she walked past like I wasn’t there. Then I gave her a candy heart and she ground it underfoot. I don’t know why it landed so hard. You’ve read more of her than I have. Tell me.
transcripts.chapter: The first question is why it hit her so hard, and I’m the wrong person to ask. Look back at what somebody else called her earlier in the book, and what she did then. The second is about a punishment. Think what sitting next to me meant after what I’d done. Not to me. To her. The third goes back over the whole week. Pick one chain, and make each link touch the next.
transcripts.wordconn: Your vocabulary answer is saved. One of this week’s words was vindictive, and Mr. Phillips used it on her in front of the whole school. Well, she wouldn’t take my apology, and she ground my candy heart to powder, so maybe he had a point. Or maybe there’s a difference between wanting revenge and refusing to be laughed at. Look at your answer and decide which word fits her better. Say why.
transcripts.workshop: Today you write five scenes, one line each. Look at what the author did with me. The whole slate business is one scene, one room, told all the way through, and it’s the only thing anybody will remember about this chapter. So when you write your five lines, don’t cram. Each scene gets one place and one thing that happens. And make the worst moment a choice somebody makes, not just bad luck.
